ENT CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • Main concern: 3-day history of loose, watery diarrhoea (≈6–7 bowel motions/day).  
  • Possible trigger: Chinese takeaway meal eaten 4 days ago.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Onset abrupt the following day; diarrhoea ongoing.  
  • Initial vomiting (now resolved), intermittent cramp-like left-lower-abdominal pain, subjective fever at onset, weakness/shakiness, loss of appetite.  
  • Able to tolerate fluids; eating only light foods/soups.
- ENT symptoms: None reported—no throat tightness, voice change, dysphagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor, dyspnoea, facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling, ear pain, or neck swelling.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: None.
- Allergies: Not documented.
- Current medications:
  • Asthma inhaler (type/dose/frequency not documented).  
  • No other regular medications; no recent antibiotics or new drugs.
- Social context:
  • Lives with wife and two children; one child vomited once without diarrhoea.  
  • Works as an accountant; has continued working despite symptoms.  
  • Non-smoker; does not drink alcohol.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: None reported.
- Airway/breathing: No stridor, dyspnoea, or noisy breathing stated.
- Mental status/associated features: Reports weakness/shakiness; otherwise alert on call.
- Vitals / examination: Not recorded (telephone consultation).
- Presence of another person: Not stated.

Assessment:
Suspected acute self-limiting infectious gastroenteritis (likely viral; bacterial food-borne infection possible).

Evidence:
• Abrupt onset watery diarrhoea, initial vomiting, low-grade subjective fever.  
• Temporal relation to recent takeaway meal; household child with brief vomiting suggests transmissible agent.

DDx (aligned with transcript):
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – most consistent with short course, watery stool, mild household spread.
2. Acute bacterial food-borne infection (e.g., Salmonella/Campylobacter) – possible given restaurant exposure; lack of blood and family clustering makes this less likely.

No ENT pathology identified; airway currently stable.

Plan:
- Conservative management: Encourage oral hydration; use oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte).  
- Symptomatic relief: Paracetamol 1 g (two 500 mg tablets) up to q6h PRN, max 4 g/day, for fever or pain.  
- Activity: Advise 2–3 days off work to rest and limit spread.  
- Red-flags/escalation: Seek medical attention if unable to keep fluids down, persistent or high fever, bloody stool or vomit, worsening abdominal pain, signs of dehydration, or no improvement within 3–4 days.  
- Follow-up: Reassessment if symptoms persist ≥4 days; consider stool culture and further evaluation.  
- Prevention/education: Safe food practices; hand hygiene emphasized. No ENT-specific interventions required.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing expected elements: formal allergy list; medication dose/frequency; recent travel history; baseline vitals; stool appearance details (mucus, color); review of ENT airway symptoms not clinically relevant but routinely collected in ENT setting.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; minimal background noise; complete history obtained for GI complaint but limited objective data due to remote setting.
